Governing with AI, Governing AI: Public Innovation and Democratic Resilience in the United States and Taiwan



Karl Ho

University of Texas at Dallas

Peter C.H. Pan

National Chung Hsing University

Prepared for presentation at the International Conference on Public Governance and Practice Forum, National Chung Hsing University, 11/7/2026.

Adoption Is Not the Same as Answerability

United States Taiwan
Public-sector AI 3,611 federal use cases (2025), up from 2,133 Generative AI authorized for civil servants since 2023
Governing instrument Executive memoranda (M-25-21, M-25-22) Framework law: AI Basic Act, in force January 2026
Latest deadline High-impact safeguards by April 2026 Agency AI risk assessments by July 2026

Both governments pair adoption with promises of trust.

Can their agencies answer for the AI they use?

Two Meanings of Governing

Governing with AI

  • Services and chatbots
  • Decision support and triage
  • Enforcement
  • Communication with citizens

Governing AI

  • Authorization and procurement
  • Testing and impact assessment
  • Disclosure and monitoring
  • Appeal, correction, withdrawal

Policy language merges them. The democratic stakes lie in how they are coupled.

Accountable Adaptive Capacity

The ability to experiment with AI, evaluate it, correct failures, and keep responsibility answerable to the public.

Component Observable in the records
Experimentation Pilot stage; pre-deployment testing
Evaluation Impact assessment; monitoring; independent review
Correction Fail-safe or human override; retirement
Answerability Named owner; notice; appeal or remedy

Resilience that keeps services running but loses contestability is organizational, not democratic, resilience.

Five Propositions

  1. Coupling: safeguards are more complete where a use has an identifiable owner and a correction route
  2. Procurement: vendor-supplied systems are less inspectable
  3. Classification discretion: new definitions narrow the scope of oversight
  4. Distributed implementation: in Taiwan, ministries with digital capacity adopt fuller rules
  5. Transfer: routines travel between systems; statutes do not

Asymmetric Evidence

United States: a public, use-by-use inventory with fields for each safeguard.

Taiwan: no equivalent inventory. Evidence comes from agency rules, procurement records, and information requests.

Our approach: give each source a distinct job.

  • US inventory → tests P1–P3 at scale
  • Procurement records (both countries) → the symmetric comparison
  • Agency rules and matched cases → P4, P5

Three levels kept apart throughout: required, reported, independently supported.

. . .

A government-wide average mostly describes three departments.

The Implementation Gap

227 deployed high-impact uses. Fewer than 1 in 5 report a completed impact assessment. 7 percent report an established appeal process.

Read the Gap Carefully

  • The inventory was compiled inside the one-year compliance window; “in progress” is the expected status.
  • The Department of Veterans Affairs reports none of the safeguard fields for its 94 deployed high-impact uses.
  • Appeal lags every other practice. It is the one tied most directly to contestability.

The 2026 inventory will show whether “in progress” became “established”.

Vendor Systems: Agency or Procurement?

Route n Mean completeness
Contracting and in-house 30 0.64
In-house development 16 0.63

But 65 of the 84 vendor uses belong to the Department of Justice, which reports everything as in progress.

The multilevel model has to separate procurement from agency.

What the Records Contain, and What They Mean

United States

  • 1,479 contract awards, FY2023–FY2026
  • 8 English search terms
  • Agency, sub-agency, vendor, amount, dates, award type, description

Taiwan

  • 2,886 tenders, 2023–2026; 2,233 full award records
  • 12 Chinese and English search terms
  • Budget, every bidder, bids and evaluation scores, award method, winner

Procurement shows governing AI at the point of purchase: who buys, from whom, through what competition.

Taiwan’s award notices name every bidder and score. Our US extract records only the winner.

Next: code contract terms for evaluation, audit and data rights (proposition P2).

How the LLM Codes Each Record

  1. Input: country + text (US description; Taiwan title and buyer), up to 2,000 characters
  2. Codebook v2: four categories with written definitions, plus AI type, function, public-facing, confidence
  3. Model: Claude Sonnet 5.5, one record per call, JSON answer only
  4. Run: 4,351 of 4,365 records coded; 1 refusal (a defense cyber award, out of scope)

. . .

Check: stratified 20% sample (882 records), coded blind by two independent coders using the written codebook (next slide).

Code: collect/20_llm_classify.py

Checking the LLM Codes

Stratified 20% sample, 882 records, coded blind and independently by two AI coders applying the written codebook.

Taiwan US Both
Records 575 307 882
Coder–coder agreement on category (Krippendorff’s α) 0.97 0.93 0.96
LLM vs coder consensus: accuracy 93% 90% 92%
LLM vs coder consensus (α) 0.90 0.75 0.87
“AI system”: precision / recall 0.97 / 0.95 0.94 / 0.95
Estimated true ÷ LLM count of AI systems 1.02 0.98

The trend holds: correcting for misclassification moves AI-system counts by 2% or less.

Weak spots: “incidental” mentions (recall 0.65–0.67); the US α of 0.75 is tentative. AI coders show consistency, not accuracy. Human coding is next.

What Governments Buy When They Buy “AI”

Taiwan’s training and consulting awards rose from 1.4 to 8.1 a month: workforce capability is being bought, not only systems.

The US mix is stable and dominated by systems.

Taiwan

A Different Architecture

  • 2023: Executive Yuan generative AI guidelines. Disclosure is required; unverified output cannot be the sole basis for decisions; AI may not draft classified documents.
  • January 2026: AI Basic Act. the National Science and Technology Council is the central authority; the Ministry of Digital Affairs leads risk classification; sector ministries write their own rules.
  • May 2026: a strategy committee chaired by the premier. Agencies complete risk assessments by July 2026 and internal controls within a year.

Implementation is distributed. The question is whether answerability is distributed with it.

What We Will Observe in Taiwan

  • Internal AI rules of about 30 central agencies, coded on the same scheme as the US inventory
  • Risk assessments (July 2026): posted versions plus Freedom of Government Information Law requests
  • 政府電子採購網 award records, 2023–2026, set against US federal contract awards
  • Public context: 64.8 percent say AI improves the quality of government services (Huang, May 2025, n = 1,171)

Design and Next Steps

Model Route

Component Data Model
A. Codebook All sources LLM-assisted coding, 20% double-coded; α ≥ 0.80
B. US inventory 2024–2025 use cases Bayesian multilevel binomial, agency intercepts
C. Procurement US and Taiwan awards Interrupted time series; contract-level models
D. Cases 4 matched cases Structured, focused comparison; process tracing

\[y_{ij} \sim \text{Binomial}(n_{ij}, \pi_{ij}), \quad \text{logit}(\pi_{ij}) = \alpha + \beta\,\text{Vendor}_{ij} + \gamma\,\text{Capacity}_j + u_j\]

Matched Cases

Two functions in each country, matched on task, population, and stakes:

  • A public-facing generative AI assistant
  • AI triage of claims or inspections, with a human making the final decision

One chain traced per case: authorize → procure → review → correct.

Timeline

When What

Jan–Mar 2027 Procurement data; Taiwan agency corpus; case documents
Mar–Apr 2027 Models; process tracing
Apr–Jun 2027 Chapter draft (8,000 words)
Jul–Sep 2027 Evidence update; 2026 US inventory

Conclusion

Adoption has outrun answerability, in different places in each system.

The US documents its gap in public. Taiwan’s is harder to observe.

The gap is widest on appeal and remedy, the practices that make AI contestable.

Democratic resilience depends less on how much AI government adopts than on whether correction and challenge are built in before deployment.

What Counts as “High-Impact” AI

OMB Memorandum M-25-21 (April 3, 2025): AI whose output serves as a principal basis for decisions or actions with a legal, material, binding or significant effect on:

  • civil rights, civil liberties or privacy
  • access to education, housing, insurance, credit, employment and other programs
  • access to critical government resources or services
  • human health and safety
  • critical infrastructure or public safety
  • strategic assets or resources, including sensitive or classified information

Presumed high-impact unless an agency documents otherwise to its Chief AI Officer: safety-critical infrastructure, law enforcement, immigration risk assessment, adjudication of federal benefits, federal hiring and firing.

Seven minimum practices, due within 365 days (April 3, 2026): pre-deployment testing · impact assessment · ongoing monitoring · operator training · human oversight · remedies or appeals · public feedback. A Chief AI Officer may waive practices for a specific application.

Replaced the 2024 categories “rights-impacting” and “safety-impacting” (M-24-10).

Coding the Inventory Fields

Field Practice Counted as established
hi_testing_conducted Pre-deployment testing Yes
hi_assessment_completed Impact assessment Yes
hi_independent_review Independent review Internal, Chief AI Officer, or board review
hi_ongoing_monitoring Monitoring Yes
hi_training_established Operator training Established
hi_failsafe_presence Fail-safe Yes (not applicable excluded)
hi_appeal_process Appeal or remedy Established (not applicable or precluded excluded)

Required only for deployed high-impact uses.

Why Not a Country Index?

  • The UN E-Government Survey does not cover Taiwan.
  • Most AI indices score national ecosystems, not public-sector governance.
  • The Government AI Readiness Index covers both countries (Taiwan ranked 4th in East Asia in 2024), but measures readiness, not answerability.

Administrative records are the better instrument for this question, with the limits of self-reports stated up front.

Who Buys AI in Taiwan

About a third of AI-titled awards come from central civilian agencies. Local governments and universities each account for roughly a quarter.

Implementation is distributed in purchasing as well as in law. A US federal comparison sees only part of this picture.

Keyword Counts Before Coding

Keyword matches inflate Taiwan’s series much more than the US one: Taiwanese titles often say “AI” for servers and workstations.

Optional Extension: A Parallel Survey Experiment

Existing opinion items differ across the two countries.

Field identical vignettes in both:

  • Human review: yes / no
  • Appeal available: yes / no
  • Disclosure of AI use: yes / no
  • Vendor or in-house system

Outcome: perceived legitimacy of the decision. This tests whether answerability features carry the same weight in both publics.
